- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially for the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp upward spikes in the history (e.g., 90+ values), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “reversion to mean” after peaks.
- Model underestimates when history shows strong downward momentum (e.g., 85–82 range) — fails to recognize the “mean reversion” or “support level” behavior.
- Forecasts are too optimistic in the short term (1–3 days) when history shows volatility — model doesn’t adjust for recent volatility or “noise”.
- Model exhibits “lag” in responding to recent price drops — often underestimates the depth of a drop until 3–5 days later.
- Model tends to “smooth” sharp transitions — fails to capture sudden drops or spikes in the true outcome, especially when they occur near the end of the 30-day window.
- When history includes a strong upward trend, model overestimates the continuation — fails to recognize “trend reversal” or “overbought” signals.
- Model underestimates when true outcome is near or below 80 — often fails to recognize “support zone” or “bottoming” behavior.
- Model overestimates when history includes a strong downward trend — fails to recognize “trend reversal” or “oversold” signals.
- Model tends to “overfit” to recent high values — forecasts are too high when recent history is high, and too low when recent history is low — exhibits “mean reversion bias”.
- Model fails to adjust for “seasonal” or “calendar” effects — e.g., price drops in late August or early September — often underestimates the drop.
